items.title: HTTP aur HTTPS: padlock asal mein kya karta hai
items.one_idea: HTTP is the plain-text request and response a browser and a server exchange; HTTPS is the same HTTP carried inside TLS, which gives three things: encryption (nobody on the way can read it), a certificate that proves the server is really that domain, and tamper detection (any change on the way is noticed).

items.hook_10s: Interviewer ने पूछा: HTTPS में padlock असल में क्या check करता है? सोचो, तुम café के WiFi पर password डाल रहे हो। बीच में कोई भी उसे पढ़ सकता है। Padlock इसी का जवाब है, और ये एक नहीं, तीन काम करता है। [frame 0: a phone and a server rack with a padlock between them; a postcard with the password written in plain letters travels along the line and a stranger's hand reads it]

hook_candidates.text: Interviewer ने पूछा: HTTPS में padlock असल में क्या check करता है?
Browser का padlock असल में क्या करता है?
Café के WiFi पर तुम्हारा password कोई भी पढ़ सकता है।

items.problem_line: Café ke WiFi pe bank ka password daalte ho, aur beech ke raaste mein koi bhi use padh sakta hai ya badal sakta hai. Padlock isi problem ko teen tareeke se rokta hai.
items.visual_idea: A phone on the left and a server rack on the right with a line between them. First a plain postcard with the password in readable letters travels along the line and a hand in the middle reads and edits it; the postcard is crossed out. Then the same postcard goes inside a locked box (encryption), the server shows an ID card that the phone checks (certificate), and a sealed tag on the box breaks if the hand touches it (tamper detection); the padlock icon in the address bar lights as the three checks tick off.
items.everyday_anchor: Sending a cheque or a parcel by courier: a plain postcard can be read by every hand it passes through; a sealed, locked box with the sender's ID checked at the door and a tamper seal is what HTTPS adds.
items.example: EXAMPLE: login on a shop site: the request carries 'password=abc123' (invented). Over HTTP the café WiFi owner could read it; over HTTPS the same bytes look like random noise to them.
facts_to_verify: HTTP is a client-server protocol: the client (browser) always starts the request, the server answers; messages are requests and responses (MDN HTTP Overview) - verified.
A request has a method (GET, POST), a path and headers; a response has a status code (such as 200) and usually a body (MDN HTTP Overview) - verified.
HTTP can run over a TLS-encrypted TCP connection; HTTPS is the encrypted version of HTTP and uses TLS to encrypt all communication between client and server (MDN Glossary HTTPS) - verified.

TLS gives encryption (data cannot be read in transit), integrity (an attacker cannot secretly modify data without detection) and authentication (the server proves it is who it claims; on the web servers usually authenticate to clients, clients usually do not) (MDN TLS) - verified.

The server's digital certificate holds a digitally signed copy of its public key and binds the key to the domain name, so the browser knows it is really talking to e.g. example.com (MDN TLS) - verified.
TLS defends against a manipulator-in-the-middle who can read and modify traffic (MDN TLS) - verified.
Say only: HTTPS hides the content, not the fact that you visited the site's address; do not claim this without a source, so leave it out unless the builder fetches one.

Do not say how the TLS handshake or key exchange works, no cipher names, no version numbers, no percentage of sites on HTTPS, no browser's padlock wording (browsers have changed it); keep HTTP request/response to method, path, status code only.
